**Scenario 1: The Moon doesn't spin at all.**
Imagine the Moon as a frozen, non-rotating block moving around Earth. The famous “man in the moon” face always points toward, say, a specific distant star. As the Moon orbits Earth once a month, people on Earth would eventually see *every* side of the Moon. There would be no “far side.” And yes, the same hemisphere would always face the Sun, creating a permanent day side and a permanent night side. This isn’t what happens.

**Scenario 2: Tidal Locking (Reality).**
The Moon makes exactly one rotation on its axis in the same time it takes to complete one orbit around Earth (about 27 days). This is synchronous rotation. Because the spin and the orbit are perfectly matched, the same face is always pointing toward Earth.

Now, think about what that spin is doing relative to the Sun.
- Grab an orange and mark an “X” on one side (the near side). Hold it at arm’s length in front of you (you’re the Earth).

**The Moon’s rotation is precisely what puts the far side in sunlight half the time.**
It spins exactly once per orbit, so relative to the Sun, it’s constantly showing a new face. A “day” on the Moon (sunrise to sunrise) is about 29.5 Earth days. So everywhere except those polar craters gets about two weeks of continuous daylight followed by two weeks of night.

So when you say, “seems like it should just stay pointed away from the light source forever”—you’re imagining a Moon that has been tidally locked to the Sun. That’s not the case.
